planetx.disclaimer: Planet Nine has not been directly confirmed. The evidence presented here represents current theoretical predictions and observational anomalies that suggest its possible existence.

overview.title: Hypothesis Overview
overview.description: The Planet Nine hypothesis proposes the existence of a large, undiscovered planet in the distant outer Solar System. This hypothetical planet could explain several observed anomalies in the orbits of distant trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs).

orbitalClustering.title: Orbital Clustering
orbitalClustering.description: Several distant TNOs share similar orbital elements (argument of perihelion, longitude of ascending node), suggesting gravitational influence from an unseen massive body.

perihelionDetachment.title: Perihelion Detachment
perihelionDetachment.description: Objects like Sedna and 2012 VP113 have perihelia far beyond Neptune's influence, which could be explained by a distant massive perturber.

solarObliquity.title: Solar Obliquity
solarObliquity.description: The ~6° tilt of the Sun's spin axis relative to the planetary orbital plane could be induced by the gravitational torque of a distant massive planet.

retrogradeOrbits.title: Retrograde TNO Orbits
retrogradeOrbits.description: The existence of high-inclination and retrograde trans-Neptunian objects can be explained by secular interactions with Planet Nine.

kuiperCliff.title: Kuiper Cliff
kuiperCliff.description: The apparent edge of the Kuiper Belt near 50 AU could be sculpted by the gravitational influence of a distant massive planet.

about.title: About OrbitScope
about.subtitle: Scientific methodology, data sources, and platform documentation

overview.title: Platform Overview
overview.description: OrbitScope is a public web tool for exploring how the sky changes in real NASA SPHEREx images. Enter an object name or coordinates and it plays every SPHEREx exposure of that spot as a short, aligned movie; it can search those images for moving objects and check every detection against NASA/JPL, Gaia and CatWISE catalogs.
overview.mission: Goal: make SPHEREx's time-domain data easy to look at for everyone, so that moving and changing objects - asteroids, comets, nearby stars and brown dwarfs - can be spotted and checked by eye.

methodology.title: Detection Methodology
methodology.step1Desc: Level-2 images are found with IRSA's TAP service (new public releases are picked up automatically), cut out around the target, zodiacal light and flagged pixels are removed.
methodology.step2Desc: Every exposure is reprojected onto one north-up grid (using the SIP-distorted WCS of each image); exposures of one survey pass are stacked by inverse variance.
methodology.step3Desc: Asteroids: a static-sky template per detector is subtracted and residuals are linked within SPHEREx's ~7-minute visits. Stars/brown dwarfs: sources are centroided in each pass and significant shifts are reported.
methodology.step4Desc: Detections are compared with known asteroids and comets from JPL SB Ident and with Gaia DR3 / CatWISE2020 stars, including their proper motions.
methodology.step5Desc: Candidates are classified (known object, new mover, stationary transient, variable) and stored; users mark them real / artifact and export the astrometry as CSV.

dataSources.title: Data Sources
dataSources.spherex: NASA SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (NASA/IPAC IRSA: TAP, datalink, IBE cutouts)
dataSources.jpl: NASA/JPL Small-Body Database, Horizons and SB Ident APIs
dataSources.mpc: CDS Sesame and NED name resolvers (object names to coordinates)
dataSources.gaia: ESA Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 (IRSA) reference catalogs
dataSources.note: All data shown in SPHEREx Blink, Sky Explorer, Detection, Comparison, Catalog and the Planet X clustering test is real and fetched live from these public services; none of them needs an API key. Literature values (Planet X evidence and predictions) are labelled as such.

limitations.title: Limitations & Disclaimers
limitations.item1: Single SPHEREx exposures reach about V≈17-18 for moving objects; fainter asteroids are usually not detected.
limitations.item2: Very bright stars saturate SPHEREx's detectors and are excluded from photometry and astrometry.
limitations.item3: The asteroid search links detections within one ~7-minute visit, so very slow movers (e.g. a distant Planet Nine) look static.
limitations.item4: Candidates are not discoveries: they need independent confirmation and must be reported through the proper channels.
limitations.item5: Planet X evidence is a published hypothesis; the clustering test here does not correct for survey selection bias.

intro.title: How it works
intro.step1: Type an object name (e.g. Barnard's Star) or RA/Dec in decimal or sexagesimal form, or pick a test target.
intro.step2: OrbitScope finds every SPHEREx exposure covering that point, removes zodiacal light, masks flagged pixels and aligns all images north-up.
intro.step3: Play the sequence. Moving objects jump between frames; variable stars change brightness. Use Difference or Motion colour to make changes pop out.
intro.note: Data: NASA SPHEREx Level-2 images via NASA/IPAC IRSA. New public releases are picked up automatically. Links are shareable and embeddable.

viewer.aria: SPHEREx image sequence. Space plays or pauses, arrow keys step through frames.
viewer.hoverHint: Hover over the image for coordinates and pixel values. Space = play/pause, ← → = step.

modeHelp.blink: Play the frames in time order.
modeHelp.difference: Current frame minus the reference frame: red = brighter now, blue = fainter now. Static stars cancel out.
modeHelp.motion: Reference frame in red, current frame in cyan. Static stars look white; moving objects show a red/cyan pair.
modeHelp.stack: Average of all frames: fainter static sources become visible, moving ones smear out.

flagHelp.PERSIST: Possible persistence from an earlier bright source

overlay.title: Catalog overlay
overlay.hint: Markers move with each star's proper motion to the date of the frame. Solid circles: > 0.2″/yr.

phot.title: Spectrum & light curve
phot.pickHint: Click on the image first to choose a position.
phot.explain: SPHEREx uses linear variable filters, so every exposure sees a source at a slightly different wavelength. Measuring the same spot in many exposures gives a 0.75–5 µm spectrum and a light curve. First run takes 1–3 minutes.
phot.noGood: All measurements are flagged (usually the source is saturated — too bright for SPHEREx). Tick 'show flagged' to see them anyway.

aladin.intro: The same field in all-sky surveys (served by NASA/IPAC IRSA): optical (DSS2), near-infrared (2MASS) and 4.6 µm (AllWISE W2, where cold brown dwarfs are brightest). Blue box: the SPHEREx cutout; pink marker: the target position at the SPHEREx epoch.

band.label: Wavelength band
band.help: SPHEREx's filters change wavelength across each detector, so every exposure sees the target at a different wavelength. A band keeps only exposures whose wavelength at the target lies inside it - e.g. CH₄ makes cold brown dwarfs fade, CO/4.6 µm makes Y dwarfs like WISE 0855 brightest.

detect.title: Moving-Object Search (real SPHEREx data)
detect.subtitle: Search real SPHEREx images for objects that move: asteroids and comets within one survey pass, or nearby stars and brown dwarfs with large proper motion across passes. Every detection is checked against known objects (JPL Small-Body database, Gaia DR3, CatWISE2020) and can be reviewed by you.

searchHelp.asteroids: Uses the individual exposures of one survey pass. Objects visible in only one visit are found by subtracting the static sky.
searchHelp.proper_motion: Uses one deep stack per survey pass (≈6 months apart). Finds sources that shifted between passes.

detect.loadingHint: A new field takes 1–3 minutes (IRSA download + JPL check). Repeating a search is much faster.
detect.how1: Pick a field (object name or coordinates) and a search type, or try an example.
detect.how2: OrbitScope downloads the real SPHEREx exposures, aligns them and builds a static-sky template per detector.
detect.how3: Residual sources that are not in the template are linked across exposures; their motion is fitted.
detect.how4: Detections are compared with known asteroids/comets (JPL) or stars (Gaia, CatWISE). Unmatched movers are new candidates — please review them.
detect.disclaimer: Candidates are not discoveries. Real objects must be confirmed with additional observations and reported through the proper channels (e.g. the Minor Planet Center).
detect.none: No candidates above the threshold in this field.
detect.noKnown: JPL lists no known asteroids or comets in this field at these times (V ≤ 21).
detect.knownNote: Positions from NASA/JPL SB Ident (geocentric). ✓ = recovered by the search. Objects fainter than V≈18 are usually below SPHEREx single-exposure depth.

explain.unknown_mover: A source seen in several exposures of one visit that is absent from the static sky and does not match any known asteroid or comet. Check it in Blink before marking it real.
explain.known_sso: Matches the predicted position of a known asteroid or comet from JPL.
explain.pm_candidate: Shifted between survey passes, but no Gaia/CatWISE star with matching motion was found here. Could be a new nearby brown dwarf — or an artifact.
explain.known_pm_star: Shifted between survey passes and matches a known star with significant proper motion.
explain.pm_unconfirmed: Shifted between passes, but the matching catalog star has little proper motion — likely a residual.
explain.variable: Brightness changed at a fixed position: a variable star or an artifact.
explain.variable_or_residual: Residual on top of a bright star; usually caused by SPHEREx's wavelength-dependent brightness, not motion.
explain.low_confidence: Detections do not fit a straight-line motion well.
explain.stationary_transient: Appears in some exposures only, but at a FIXED position (it recurs in other visits or did not move between visits). Solar-system objects always move, so this is a variable source, detector persistence or another artifact.
explain.target_measurement: The requested target itself, measured in every survey pass even when it is too faint for the blind search. Its motion is compared with the catalog proper motion below.

targetCheck.title: Target motion check
targetCheck.confirmed: Motion confirmed: detected at ≥3σ and agrees with the catalog.
targetCheck.agreesWeak: Agrees with the catalog, but below 3σ — more survey passes will sharpen it.
targetCheck.disagrees: Measured motion does not agree with the catalog value.
targetCheck.noCatalog: No catalog proper motion for comparison.

detect.rejected: Not counted as a mover because

reject.no_steady_motion: points scatter around one spot instead of moving steadily
reject.scatter: positions scatter more than their measurement error
reject.flux_jump: brightness jumps by more than 3× between exposures
reject.missing_in_visit: a bright source missing from most exposures of its visit
reject.edge: too close to the image edge

planetxLive.subtitle: The Planet Nine hypothesis, tested on live orbits from NASA/JPL. The clustering statistics on this page are computed by OrbitScope; the evidence cards and predicted parameters are literature values.
planetxLive.testTitle: Is the orbital clustering real? (live JPL orbits)
planetxLive.testIntro: Every distant detached TNO in the JPL Small-Body Database (a ≥ 150 AU, q ≥ 30 AU, well-determined orbit) is fetched right now. The Rayleigh test asks whether their orbital angles point in a preferred direction more than chance would allow.
planetxLive.periPlot: Perihelion directions (q·cos ϖ, q·sin ϖ) - dashed line: mean direction
planetxLive.periNote: If orbits were randomly oriented, the points would surround the Sun evenly. They bunch around ϖ ≈ {{mean}}°.
planetxLive.caveat: Surveys only find distant TNOs where and when they looked, so observational selection can create apparent clustering. Analyses that model survey biases (Shankman et al. 2017; Napier et al. 2021) find the clustering consistent with no Planet Nine. This test does not correct for selection bias.
planetxLive.table: Orbit table ({{n}} objects; grey = poorly determined orbit, not used)
planetxLive.missing: {{n}} object(s) could not be fetched right now
planetxLive.spherexTitle: Could SPHEREx or OrbitScope find Planet Nine?
planetxLive.spherexText: Predicted Planet Nine is very faint (likely V ≈ 20–24) and, at 300–500 AU, moves only ~0.3″ per hour, mostly from Earth's own motion. OrbitScope's asteroid search links detections inside a ~7-minute SPHEREx visit, so such a slow mover looks static and would not be detected; a dedicated multi-day search would be needed. This is an honest limitation of the current tool.
planetxLive.literature: Literature summary - not measured by OrbitScope.
planetxLive.predSource: Brown & Batygin (2021), AJ 162:219 - literature values, not measured here.
planetxLive.compareTitle: Does the result depend on which objects you pick?
planetxLive.sampleComplete: Complete: all JPL objects, orbit quality ≤ {{cc}}
planetxLive.sampleLiterature: Literature: the objects discussed in Planet Nine papers
planetxLive.compareNote: Both samples are fetched live from JPL. The hand-picked literature sample clusters much more strongly than the complete, objectively selected sample — a direct look at how object selection affects the Planet Nine evidence.
planetxLive.periLegend: Orange: objects of the literature sample.
planetxLive.ccHelp: JPL orbit condition code: 0 = best determined, 9 = most uncertain. Objects above 5 (grey) are not used.
